The Planning Board requests the initiation of the attached zoning amendments in order to allow residential adaptive reuse of accessory structures by Special Permit. The zoning amendment includes a new section in the “Special Regulations” article, as well as amendments to the “Use Regulations.” Recently, two local landowners have met with the Planning Director to inquire about converting existing accessory structures into residential units either for themselves or their family. The Planning Director proposed an amendment to the existing ADU ordinance to allow for ADUs larger than 900 square feet by Special Permit. However, the proposal to reconsider the ADU ordinance was met with pushback. Therefore, the draft amendment below is independent of the ADU ordinance – it is a new zoning ordinance to allow for existing accessory structures, such as barns or carriage houses, built before August 2016 to be converted into single-family homes by Special Permit. The City of Greenfield is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity Employer, a designated Green Community and a recipient of the “Leading by Example” Award Note: Text with a strikethrough is text to be deleted, black bold italic text is newly proposed text. ---ARTICLE VII ~ 200-7.22. Adaptive Residential Reuse of Accessory Structures A. Purpose. The purpose of this Section is to allow the adaptive reuse of existing accessory structures, such as barns, carriage houses, garages, and other structures for residential purposes in any zoning district where residential uses are allowed. This zoning provides for adaptive residential reuse of accessory structures to accomplish the following purposes: (1) Enable homeowners to utilize existing structures on their land for rental income and alternative living options; (2) Support the maintenance of and prevent dilapidation of historical structures; (3) Increase housing options with gentle density that maintains the existing fabric of the built environment; (4) B. Ensure safe and healthy housing compliant with the Building Code. Applicability. (1) See Sections 200-4.1 through 200-4.17 and Appendix A, Table of Uses, for permitting requirements. C. Adaptive Residential Reuse Standards. The Zoning Board of Appeals, acting as the special permit granting authority (SPGA), may grant a special permit to use an existing accessory structure for single-family residential use on a lot with any number of existing dwellings, provided all of the following conditions are satisfied: (1) The accessory structure must have existed continuously since before August 2016 and have a minimum gross floor area of 900 square feet. (2) The accessory structure may be converted to no more than one dwelling unit and must be a complete, separate housekeeping unit containing both kitchen and bath. The City of Greenfield is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity Employer, a designated Green Community and a recipient of the “Leading by Example” Award (3) The accessory structure may not expand in gross floor area or footprint, except for improvements related to fire safety, ADA accessibility, or utilities. (4) The accessory structure may be converted to residential use notwithstanding nonconformity with dimensional requirements, provided that the conversion does not increase the degree of nonconformity. (5) The accessory structure must be and remain located on the same lot. (6) The exterior façade of the accessory structure shall substantially retain its appearance and architectural features shall be preserved to the maximum extent practicable. (7) The construction of any residential unit must be in conformity with the State Building Code, Title V of the State Sanitary Code, 527 CMR – MA Fire Prevention Regulations and other local ordinances and regulations. (8) Prior to issuance of a permit, a floor plan must be submitted showing the proposed interior and exterior changes to the building. (9) For dwellings to be served by on-site septic system, the owner must obtain a letter from the Board of Health stating that the existing sewage disposal system is adequate for the proposed residential use before a Building Permit can be obtained. (10) In order to encourage the development of housing units for disabled and handicapped individuals and persons with limited mobility, the Inspector of Buildings or Zoning Board of Appeals may allow reasonable deviation from the stated conditions where necessary to install features that facilitate access and mobility for disabled persons. (11) Adaptive residential reuse of accessory structures shall not be used for short-term rentals. EAT | EXPANDED ACCESSIBLE TRANSPORTATION Expanding Accessible Transportation – Bedford and Beyond History needs service design and funding options SB Companion to Expanded Accessible Transportation Presentation | October 25, 2026 Purpose and recommendation Expanded Accessible Transportation (EAT) would connect Bedford residents with medical care in Bedfordadjacent communities while preserving Bedford Local Transit (BLT) for established in-town travel. This report explains the transportation gap, the history of efforts to address it, the proposed service and the resources needed to operate it. It is intended for residents, Council on Aging (COA) Board members, and Town staff reviewing the proposal. The recommendation adds a staffed accessible vehicle and a driver working 26 hours per week. EAT would be available to the community, with priority for older residents and persons with disabilities. Wheels of Life, The RIDE, and the launched Uber Health pilot would continue to serve complementary needs. The proposed service emphasizes dependable medical journeys, including the return home, and reduced reliance on family members who may be working, live elsewhere, or lack an accessible vehicle. The current planning position Item Planning amount Vehicle purchase $90,258 Annual salary and operations before benefits (based on FY26) $37,587 One-time parking lot shelter $1,250 Existing Town staffing funds reallocated $10,294 Supplemental Transit Grant expansion allocation $14,964 (est. FY2028) Annual Town investment before benefits and fares $12,329 Using a salary of $33,314, the current net annual Town planning estimate is $12,329 before benefits, additional fare revenue, and other unpriced costs. First-year base requests, excluding a vehicle shelter, are $12,329 with the vehicle grant and $89,048 without the vehicle grant. Adding the one-time $1,250 shelter produces complete first-year requests of $13,579 and $90,298, respectively. Both scenarios retain the $13,539 COA formula-grant contribution, or 15% of the vehicle cost. Benefits and grant accounting remain subject to Town Finance review. The historical March 2026 MassDOT vehicle award supports the project history but does not guarantee a future award. EAT is presented as a proposed Town priority; final service, funding, and operating decisions would follow the appropriate Town process. Bedford has several transportation resources, but they do not consistently provide the same complete journey: appropriate geography, accessible equipment, affordable payment, and a dependable return. October 2026 | 1 EAT | EXPANDED ACCESSIBLE TRANSPORTATION Guide and Principal Findings The central gap is a usable medical journey beyond Bedford: an appropriate vehicle, a driver, an affordable payment arrangement and a dependable return. A resident may have several nominal transportation options yet lack one that meets all four conditions. Requested Select Board support This report asks the Select Board to recognize expanded accessible transportation as a Town priority and support Town staff advancing both FY2028 funding pathways in parallel: the vehicle-grant pathway and a Townfunded vehicle pathway if grant funding is unavailable or delayed. Advancing both pathways keeps a single acquisition decision open while preserving the Town’s ability to act promptly if grant timing or award conditions create a delay. Final appropriations, procurement, and operating policies would remain subject to the appropriate Town processes. Finding Why it matters 24 of 46 BLT survey respondents requested regional medical rides 52.2% selected out-of-town medical transportation as an improvement. [2] Wheels of Life received 22 responses from 40 invitees All 22 rated it important or very important. Nine of 20 reported missing, delaying or cancelling care because of transportation limitations. [28] Existing financial assistance has limits Wheels of Life offers up to $500 per calendar year. The Uber Health pilot offers $10 on up to four one-way rides per month. [38] Reading guide The report proceeds from history and existing services to separate local surveys, DASH lessons and regional evidence. It then describes the intended population, road safety and operating model, followed by the three fictional rider profiles. The financial sections explain capital, annual operations, offsets, and illustrative fares. The final sections address Board options, implementation, evaluation, common questions and source documentation. The report brings together the history, resident experience, service alternatives and financial structure of the proposed expansion. Its purpose is to explain why the gap exists and how a staffed, accessible service could address it. Operating counts in this report use one-way passenger trips; a person travelling out and back generates two trips. Fictional rider profiles also show round trips explicitly. Passenger seats, unique riders and trips per day are different measures. Surveys retain their own populations and question denominators. Fiscal years run July through June. FY2028 is July 1, 2027–June 30, 2028; FY2029 follows one year later. Wheels of Life resident allowances follow the calendar year. Dollar amounts are shown precisely in the financial sections. The estimated annual salary is $33,314; benefits remain to be confirmed by Town Finance. TRANSPORTATION 1 History and the Current Decision Bedford has considered additional transportation capacity for more than a decade. Reporting in December 2013 described BLT as close to maximum use and discussed Carleton-Willard medical taxi support. The present proposal builds on that history, including the DASH regional pilot and the 2018 aging needs assessment. [11, 21] Period Milestone 2015 Economic Development Coordinator Alyssa Sandoval presented an expanded transit proposal following Healthy Bedford work. [14] Spring 2016 Finance Committee recommended a pilot; Annual Town Meeting approved Article 21. [15, 16] August and September 2016 Select Board awarded the operating contract August 8. DASH service began September 12. [17, 18] June 2018 Aging in Bedford documented driving adaptations, transportation satisfaction and caregiver concerns. [21] June 30, 2019 DASH ended after a third operating year. Healthy Bedford administered its final year. [20] 2024 The current operating-grant framework was completed, according to the recent COA planning update. Expanded-service funding has not yet been used for the proposed expansion. March 13, 2026 MassDOT notified Bedford of an award for one Type A van, with an estimated $13,539 (15%) local match. [39] July to September 2026 Updated Wheels of Life funding and surveys, the Uber Health pilot and new operating-offset information inform the current proposal. [35, 38] What the historical award establishes The March 13 email concerned the FY26 Community Transit Grant Program. It reported 131 vans awarded out of 238 requested and stated that final award and match values would follow after inflation adjustment. These are vehicle counts, not numbers of communities. [39] The COA project history identifies FY2027, beginning July 1, 2026, as the intended service start. It reports that the vehicle could not be accepted because the request did not obtain inclusion on the Annual Town Meeting warrant. This should not be described as a Town Meeting vote rejecting the vehicle. The next application needs an explicit path connecting grant acceptance, local authorization and annual operating support. October 2026 | 4 EAT | EXPANDED ACCESSIBLE TRANSPORTATION 2 How the Proposal Evolved The starting point is the purpose of the service: residents need usable access to scheduled medical care outside Bedford, while the local service must remain dependable. EAT identifies the proposed expansion in service; the vehicle and driver are the resources required to deliver it. A regional need within a local system BLT, Wheels of Life, and the former DASH pilot

The Pledge of Allegiance was recited. Chair Pavidis called for a moment of silence for Anapum Wali who recently passed. 1. Open Microphone Janet Moran of 218 Rangeway Road #294 – Ms. Moran stated that she would like to speak about Article 38. She is President of Phase II and a Town Meeting member. Last year, the Select Board and Planning Board voted against a development at Swanson Meadows. They are allowed to build 40-45 single family homes and now they are asking for a zoning overlay to build condos. Last year, they wanted 192 units and this concept plan is showing 160 units. This is a conceptual plan only and they are using stock photos. They will maximize the site and traffic and noise will be substantial. They will have to cut 1,000 trees and they will eliminate green space. Michael Pendleton/Dick Coluantoni - Mr. Pendleton stated that he wanted to speak about Anapum Wali who just passed way. Mr. Wali was a ZBA member for 10 years and he was a bright and valued individual. He asked that the Select Board send a letter to his wife in appreciation of his service. He will be missed. Grace Tucci of 7 Carson Street – Ms. Tucci stated that she would like an update on the audit and website for the next meeting. She would also like the recordings of the boards and committees updated on the website. Prakash Gound of 218 Rangeway Road #211– Mr. Gound stated that he is against the rezoning for Swanson Meadows. Pallavi Dedlia of 216 Rangeway Road, #193 – Mr. Dedlia stated that it is not clear on the zoning change for Swanson Meadows will affect us. There also seems like there are legal issues. What happens to the clubhouse if the golf course goes away. There is a noise issue now with the clubhouse. If this is on Parcel A and B, would this be spot zoning? MOTION - Member Rosa made a motion to send a letter to Anapa Wali’s family, thanking them for his service. The motion was seconded by Secretary Darris-O’Connor and unanimously voted 5-0-0. Rose Chersiykski of 218 Rangeway Road #1104 – Ms. Chersiykski stated that she is a trustee of the condo association. There are 76% of residents opposed to this and they are requesting that this not be recommended to Town Meeting. There is a conservation restriction that is in perpetuity. The zoning doesn’t change that. There is toxic waste, sewer problems, traffic, wetlands and noise. Ms. Moran spoke again and asked what happens with the clubhouse because it’s so noisy now. This would be spot zoning according to Kelley Sardina. Announcements 2. Vacancies on Boards and Committees Secretary Darris-O’Connor read the vacancies on Boards and Committees. 3. Attorney DeRensis stated that they have been Billerica’s Town Counsel for a year and a few months. We’ve been operating under a retainer system, but they are willing to negotiate as long as it works for both sides. Our rates are 20% less than Harrington Heep. We took over from your previous Town Counsel, and it took longer and was more difficult than it should have been. It was a hard transition. There was a flood of backlogs and many upheavals. There have been changes in the Town Manager, in Select Board Chairs as well as many disputes between Board members. They have hired Attorney Moreira as Billerica’ point of contact. They have accomplished a lot for the Town and have had success in courts. We have invested a lot of time in Billerica and with our reputation, there is no need to go elsewhere. We have 20 lawyers and 9 paralegals, and we just hired a 30-year experienced land use attorney. Our Real Estate department with 7 attorneys will be available to Billerica. John Ruggieri joined the meeting via Zoom. They also have Attorney Clements on staff that have over 30 years’ experience in land use and zoning matters. Member Rosa stated that when you took over from KP Law, you said that they did not provide a lot of our files and you had to recreate them. We asked you to track the time separately, but you never did that. This was frustrating because we made it very clear that we wanted to try to recoup that. There have been issues like with AT&T lease on the water tower. This was sent to Attorney Hucksam, and he didn’t do anything about it. He likes that the cost is less, but they have spent significantly more than what we have paid in the past. Before Mr. Dillon came, no one was reviewing what was covered by the retainer. Secretary Darris-O’Connor thanked them for coming but to be honest, he has dire concerns that Brooks and DeRensis can represent Billerica. Does Brooks & DeRensis have a dedicated municipal law unit. Attorney DeRensis stated that everyone is a municipal law member, but we do other private business but we can handle a wide range of issues. Secretary Darris-O’Connor asked how many towns you represent. Attorney DeRensis replied seven towns with 20 lawyers. Harrington Heep represents 27 towns with 13 lawyers. Secretary Darris-O’Connor stated that we need timely responses. There was a question asked about the reorganization of the Select Board, and it took over a week to answer. Attorney DeRensis stated that every Select Board member has access to Town Counsel and we were getting conflicting information and politics aside, we did provide legal opinions. Secretary Darris-O’Connor asked why there were multiple opinions on the preliminary warrant. Attorney DeRensis stated that they were editing articles and they did not get the full story. Secretary Darris-O’Connor stated that we need timely opinions regardless of who asks. Secretary Darris-O’Connor stated that at Town Meeting there was a motion to move the question and was asked if a simple majority vote was required or a 2/3 vote and we couldn’t get a clear answer. Attorney DeRensis stated that this dealt with MBTA and it was a not a clear issue. Vice Chair Burrows stated that he is concerned with response time with department heads. He doesn’t want a personal opinion; he wants to know what the law is. When bad information is given, it drops your credibility. The bills have been astronomical, and he wonders what is covered under the retainer. Attorney DeRensis stated that they put Attorney Moreira in charge of getting timely answers and early on it was a flood gate. There are changing opinion because we are not given all the relevant information and we need to give an opinion based on the information given. Vice Chair Burrows stated that the Chair was supposed to be cc’d on every email and that was not happening. Attorney DeRensis agreed that was an issue and we fixed that. Member Favreau prefaced her comments that the opinion for the preliminary warrant was thorough. You’re firm has not been responsive in the last six months. We met in January in Executive Session to discuss deficiencies. Some issues have improved but some haven’t. What would your firm do differently if selected. Attorney DeRensis stated that we have provided tracking for questions received and we provide it weekly. Member Favreau stated that she hasn’t seen that. Chair Pavidis stated that it goes to herself and the Town Manager. She can send it to the entire Board. Member Favreau asked what would be done differently. There are issues with response time, different opinions, lack of trust, accuracy of law. Attorney DeRensis stated that we are told one story and then someone comes to us with different information, it’s hard to give an accurate opinion. Member Favreau asked what the recommendation would be moving forward because we need adequate legal counsel. There have been some improvements but not quite enough. Attorney DeRensis stated that the full board should get the tracking log and sometimes the law is not clear. Mr. Dillon stated that you have 20 attorneys representing 7 towns but how many municipal attorneys are on staff. Attorney DeRensis replied 16. Mr. Dillon asked how many do only municipal law. Attorney DeRensis replied 6. Mr. Dillon asked if you are not selected, what is the transition plan. Attorney DeRensis replied that they would never do what KP Law did and will always protect the town. Chair Pavidis stated that there have been a lot of changes. What happens when five Select Board members have facts that they believe are true. The response time has improved but is still lacking. Attorney DeRensis stated that the Board should use the Town Manager as a clearing house. All correspondence should go through the Town Manager, and the Town Manager would send it to Town Counsel. Member Rosa stated that per our policies and procedures, both the Town Manager and Town Counsel are appointed by this Board. Our policies require that the Chair and Town Manager be copied on all emails to Town Counsel. If you receive conflicting questions, reach out to Town Manager. Member Rosa asked if Brooks & DeRensis has the bandwidth to handle Billerica. Attorney DeRensis replied yes. 4 Meeting Held - 365 Boston Road, Billerica, MA 01821 – 978-671-0939 www.town.billerica.ma.us TOWN OF BILLERICA SELECT BOARD MINUTES SEPTEMBER 22, 2025 Attorney DeRensis stated that they are willing to work with the Town on the policies and procedures and with the retainer. On motion by Vice-President Jadczak and seconded by Councilor Markee, it was unanimously voted to suspend Public Speak to allow for Mayor Derby to present information regarding the proposed Special Election. Public Hearing – Supplemental Appropriation for $5,000.00 from Free Cash to fund a new parttime position in the Tax Collector’s Office for FY26 President Denham stated that this item was removed from the agenda without prejudice. It was stated that the individual was hired before funds were appropriated. Mayor Derby spoke regarding the request for the part-time position in the Tax Collector’s Office. He stated that there is a desperate need for the position. If collections get behind, it affects the Treasurer and Auditor. He said that the position will be covered by Enterprise Funds in the future since the employee will be handling water bills. Vice-President Jadczak said that while she is in support of getting assistance in the Collector’s Office, she asked why it was not previously mentioned by the Mayor or Human Resources that the person has already been hired. Mayor Derby said that because the position will be funded through Enterprise Funds it is not at risk for paying unemployment. Human Resources Director Emily Russo stated that the city will now implement requisition forms to assure that funding is in place before employees are hired. On mo on by Councilor Kwiecinski and seconded by Councilor Schmidt, it was unanimously voted to set a public hearing for the supplemental appropria on request for $5,000.00 from Free Cash to fund a new part- me posi on in the Tax Collector’s Oﬃce for FY 26 for May 11, 2026 at 6:15 p.m. at 50 Payson Avenue, second ﬂoor, in City Council Chambers. Mayor’s Request for the City Council to set a Special Election for June 9, 2026 for a vote of a proposed Tax Levy Override of $6,900,000.00 President Denham asked Mayor Derby to speak to this before Public Speak. 1 Mayor Derby stated that since COVID, budgets have been growing in relation to inflation. Over the last few years, the city has been utilizing stabilization money along with other one-time funds to balance the budget. The city was without a Treasurer for approximately a year, a new Treasurer was hired in August. He said that Free Cash was certified in March when it usually happens in October/November of the previous year. He added that debt and interest figures came in significantly higher than anticipated. Mayor Derby stated that the requested amount of $6.9 million will allow the city to not have to request another override next year. Public Comment Summary: Dan Rist, 26 Line Street, was a 27-year member of the City Council and was on the Finance Commitee for 20 years. He said that he wants to “lend credibility” to what this budget situa on is: increase in inﬂa on, increase in health care costs. He said that what the number requested is up to you, but he wants to only put one number on the ballot. He said the city will lose a lot of teachers, the School Department is half of the city’s budget. There will be decreases in response me from the Fire and Police Departments. The Senior Center and Nonotuck Park have reduced hours. He said that a “No” vote is extremely dangerous. William Joss, 60 Division Street, said that he wants people to know that this is an ongoing expense. He ques oned how the city could not have a Treasurer and get into this situa on. Cathy Wauczinski, Overlook Drive, said that the property tax increase will also increase the amount residents pay in CPA (Community Preserva on Act) tax. She said that a water rate increase was approved by the Board of Public Works. She said that the City Council, School Commitee, and former Mayor are responsible for this. She said that Easthampton Ac ve Ci zens will pe on to remove the CPA tax. Darlene Orvieto, Muter Street, said that there have been mistakes by the Governor and former Mayor. She said there should not be an override vote un l “we can see the budget.” Mateusz Marcinowski, 7 West Lake Street, said that his son is a recipient of special educa on. He said that he supports the override and how important it is but realizes that this is not an easy choice for anyone. James Ramsey, Campbell Drive, said that he has lived in Easthampton his en re life me. He asked where the state and cannabis funds are. He said that Main Street is not in good condi on and added that he lives within his means. Nori Torman, 52 East Street, said that “charity begins at home” and that Easthampton is our home. 2 ? Lavalley, Maxine Circle, said that they are impressed with the City Council in its considera on of senior ci zens. They said that many people cannot aﬀord to re re and may lose their homes. They asked if there is another way to resolve this. Jess Atkins-Barber, 22 Vadnais Street, is a tenth grader at Easthampton High School. They would like us to stay connected as a community and to move forward on the override. Kathleen Joss, 60 Division Street, said that she is concerned about the increase of 6-8 more liquor licenses. She said that she frequently walks and that there is a lot of speeding in Easthampton, adding that there was an accident on Northampton Street today. Carol Brodeur, 72 Oliver Street, said that we need to live within our budget and make cuts. She stated that she is against the override. Chris O’Connor, 21 Ashley Circle, said she is opposed to the override, sta ng that elected oﬃcials need to balance the budget. Jen Sandler, 26 Williston Avenue, said that she does not know exactly how we got here, saying that inﬂa on is more than 2 ½ %. She asked if the city could involve ci zens more regularly in hopes that this will lead to a more democra c discussion. Karl Prahl, 15 Torrey Street, said that the city needs to look at diﬀerent sources of revenue. Carolyn Cushing, Main Street, said that it seems important to have the override and hear people’s voices. She said that there are challenges with communica ng the ballot ques on if it is a “pyramid” type. Sam Hunter, 8 Mayher Street, member of the Easthampton School Commitee, asked the City Council to vote to set the Special City Elec on for the override. Sam said that some programs such as the summer food program may have to be cut next year. Dan Zdonek, member of the Easthampton Board of Assessors, but stated that he is not represen ng the Board. He said that he has seen a rough dra of the numbers and it does not look good. He said that the vote should set the number at $6.9 million and a lower number that might pass if the City Council feels that $6.9 million is too high. He said that if informa on does not get out, the override will not pass. President Denham addressed some of the ques ons posed during Public Speak. Why was there no Treasurer for a signiﬁcant amount of me? The last Treasurer le during the previous administra on for personal reasons and the eﬀort to ﬁll the posi on took a signiﬁcant amount of me. 3 Regarding the proposed 6-8 addi onal liquor licenses, this is a way for restaurants to raise revenue since the markup on food is very small. In response to a ques on of the meline, why only a month to ﬁgure this out? Free Cash was cer ﬁed in March. Public Speak con nued Liz Perry, Precinct 3, ques oned why budgets are being proposed to be cut by the size of the department’s budget rather than its importance to the community? Julie Slavet, 14 Nicols Way, (online) said that local property tax is not a good way to support local government. She added that it would have been useful to have some visual aids at the mee ng such as slides. She asked for a task force on revenue to be set up. Leslie Sharr, Nashawannuck Street, said that the override will aﬀect everyone including landlords increasing rent. She asked that the library not be part of the proposed cuts. Sean Abbot, Summer Street, (online) said that this was not brought on by us and will be diﬃcult for folks but cuts will also be diﬃcult. Leslie Buton, 5 Fox Run, said that she has a lot of experience managing budgets at a signiﬁcant level. She asked about contractual costs such as the level of increases for teachers’ contracts. Councilor Kwiecinski asked if the meline is ght because the budget is scheduled to be out soon. Mayor Derby said that the schools have a statutory deadline to let teachers know by June 15th if they are going to be re-hired for the following school year. He added that the city budget needs to be passed by July 1st. On mo on by Councilor Peake and seconded by Councilor Jamrog-McQuaid it was unanimously voted to set a Special City Elec on on June 9, 2026 to vote on a Proposi on 2 ½ Override Ques on reques ng $6,900,000.00. Councilor Peake retracted his mo on and Councilor Jamrog-McQuaid retracted his second of the mo on. Mo on was made by Councilor Peake and seconded by Councilor Jamrog-McQuaid to set a Special City Elec on for June 9, 2026. The ballot ques on shall read as follows: “Shall the City of Easthampton be allowed to assess an addi onal $6,900,000 in real estate and personal property taxes for the purposes of opera ng the Municipal Government and Public Schools for the ﬁscal year beginning July ﬁrst, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six?” 4 Mo on was made by Councilor Kwiecinski and seconded by Councilor Peake to amend the mo on to add an addi onal ques on of reques ng $3,450,000.00 in real estate and personal property taxes for purposes of opera ng the Municipal Government and Public Schools for the ﬁscal year beginning July ﬁrst, Two Thousand and Twenty Six? Councilor Peake inquired of Councilor Kwiecinski how he arrived at the amount of $3,450,000.00. Councilor Kwiecinski said that the amount he proposed is “closer in line” to the amount the city is using from reserves. He said that this is one half of the amount proposed of $6,900,000.00. He added that in reviewing override ques ons from other communi es, most had two op ons on the ballot. Councilor Peake said that in theory he is not opposed to a second amount but if the city proposes two ques ons on the ballot, there will be a very short meline to educate voters. In a pyramid type ques on, if both ques ons pass, the larger number prevails. People may think that the city is asking for both amounts which is a concern that has played out in other communi es. Councilor Peake asked the Mayor if the City Council wants to propose a separate, lower number, would this require three diﬀerent budgets? Mayor Derby replied, that “yes” he would meet with department heads again for a third round of budgets. Councilor Kwiecinski said that he “wants to put on record” that he is amenable to another second number, he is not ed to the amount he proposed. Councilor Peake stated that he wants to use a number that has a ra onale behind it. Councilor Newton asked Mayor Derby if $3.9 million would cover the city for the next year. Mayor Derby responded that there would s ll be signiﬁcant cuts. Mayor Derby said that approximately $4.5 million was used to balance the budget. With the proposed amount of $3.9 million there will be a signiﬁcant gap and that they city would be back reques ng another override. President Denham said that we have a mo on and second on the amendment. Vice-President Jadczak said that one concern with op ons on the ballot is that if the lower number passes and the city has to come back reques ng more funds, this will not look good. Councilor Newton said that she is comfortable with one number considering what everyone else has said. 5 Councilor Schmidt said that he does not want to give the impression that the lower number will ﬁx things long-term. Councilor Markee said that he is not comfortable with any amount below $6.9 million, sta ng that this is the lower number considering an amount between $8 million and $8.5 million is closer to what it necessary to give the city 4-5 years of ﬁscal stability. A vote was taken on the mo on for the Proposi on 2 ½ ballot ques on to request $3,450,000.00 and the mo on failed with 7 against, 2 in favor. Councilor Peake said that year a er year we have passed budgets to keep the level of service from the previous year but with costs increasing. He said that many communi es are dealing with overrides now. He referenced the Massachusets Municipal Associa on (MMA) ar cle “The Perfect Storm” detailing how many ci es and towns are now in the same situa on and how state aid has not kept up with costs. President Denham said that this is a par cularly diﬃcult conversa on to have. She said that she was the only Councilor to not vote for the budget last year because she did not want to take $4.5 million from the stabiliza on fund. President Denham said that this pains her and that there will be people who cannot aﬀord the override and will be forced to leave the community. President Denham asked Councilor Peake, as Finance Commitee Chair, to meet with the City Auditor more frequently. The vote returned to the main mo on of a request for $6.9 million. On mo on by Councilor Peake and seconded by Councilor Kwiecinski it was unanimously voted to set a Special City Elec on for June 9, 2026 for a Proposi on 2 ½ Override Ques on as follows: “Shall the City of Easthampton be allowed to assess an addi onal $6,900,000 in real estate and personal property taxes for the purposes of opera ng the Municipal Government and Public Schools for the ﬁscal year beginning July ﬁrst, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six?” On motion by Councilor Kwiecinski and seconded by Councilor Smith it was unanimously voted that this meeting adjourn. Town Hall, 334 Main Street Great Barrington, MA 01230 Telephone: (413) 528-1619 Fax: (413) 528-2290 TOWN OF GREAT BARRINGTON MASSACHUSETTS ___ PLANNING BOARD October 29, 2026 Zoning Board of Appeals Town Hall 334 Main Street Great Barrington, MA RE: 110 Cottage Street Dear Members of the ZBA: At its meeting of October 22, 2026, the Planning Board voted to send a favorable recommendation for the application filed by James Toby Zucco for permission to construct a larger garage on the same nonconforming footprint as the previous structure at 110 Cottage Street, Great Barrington, per Sections 5.7 and 10.4 of the zoning bylaws. Thank you for your attention to this matter. Sincerely, Kimberly L. Shaw Kimberly L. Shaw Planning Board Secretary Cc: Chris Rembold, Assistant Town Manager & Director of Planning and Development Town of Great Barrington Town Manager’s Office www.townofgbma.gov 334 Main Street, Great Barrington, MA 01230 (413) 528‐1619 lhartsgrove@townofgbma.gov Liz Hartsgrove Town Manager ___ Chris Rembold Assistant Town Manager Memo To: Zoning Board or Appeals Members From: Date: Liz Hartsgrove, Town Manager October 28, 2026 Re: Cc: 110 Cottage Street Special Permit Recommendation Selectboard Members The Great Barrington Selectboard, at its meeting on October 26, 2026, voted unanimously (5‐0) to send a positive recommendation of the Special Permit application from James Toby Zucco to construct a larger garage on the same nonconforming footprint as the previous structure at 110 Cottage St, Great Barrington, per Sections 5.7 and 10.4 of the zoning bylaw. Zoning Board of Appeals Town of Great Barrington Minutes of Monday, July 27, 2026 The following members were present: JB Brodeur, Stephen McAlister, Madonna Meagher, Peter Most, and Michael Wise. James Manning (alternate) was not present. Also Present: Assistant Town Manager/Planning Director Christopher Rembold. 150 Hurlburt Road: application for a Variance Chair Peter Most reopened the hearing at 3:00 pm, noting that the case was continued from June 30. The hearing was on this agenda because the continuation originally scheduled for July 21 could not occur due to the agenda not being timely posted. Most opened the public hearing and invited the applicant to present the project. Most noted that since June 30, the state has passed a new law that changed the criteria for Variances in MGL Ch 40A section 10. He said the new law became effective July 1 and lowers the threshold for variances to a standard of “practical difficulty.” He said the board received the applicant’s written response as to how the proposal meets the Variance criteria. He said that it is written based on the previous criteria, but the board must use the new standard per the law currently in effect. Applicant Max Ritt described the proposal and reviewed the additional information he sent to the Board based on the last session. It is made part of the record of the permit. Board members discussed the applicant’s responses, referencing the new criteria of Section 10 as follows: (i) whether the practical difficulty relates to soil conditions, shape or topography of such land or structures; Members agreed that the nonconforming lot shape and the placement of the well and the septic system make it practically difficult to place the garage in a conforming location behind the existing house. (ii) whether the strict enforcement would impose a financial hardship on the appellant or petitioner; Members agreed based on the information provided that the cost to move the well and the septic system in order to build the garage in a conforming location would be a financial hardship. (iii) whether the benefit sought by the appellant or petitioner can be achieved by some other method feasible for the appellant or petitioner to achieve; and Members agreed there was no other method feasible to locate the garage. (iv) whether the practical difficulty was self-created. Members agreed the current owner and applicant did not locate the existing structure or utilities and therefore did not self create the practical difficulties. Most said if he had to decide the Variance based on the old criteria he would have been skeptical but believes the applicant meets the current criteria. Brodeur and Meagher agreed. McAlister agreed stating the Exhibit A provided to the board tells the story clearly. Wise said the changes in the law make all the difference in this case. Wise moved to close the hearing. Meagher seconded. On a roll call vote, all were in favor. ZBA Minutes July 27, 2026 Wise moved that the strict enforcement of the front and side yard setbacks of the R2 zone does result in a practical difficulty for the proposal, based on the discussion of the four criteria. Meagher seconded. On a roll call vote, all were in favor. Citizen Speak: None Adjourn: Most adjourned the meeting at approximately 3:40 PM. Minutes taken by: Christopher Rembold 2

Town of Hamilton Select Board Meeting Minutes of September 14, 2026 ___ Pursuant to the Open Meeting Law, MGL Chapter 30 A, §§ 18-25, written notice posted by the Town Clerk delivered to all Select Board members, a meeting of the Hamilton Select Board was posted for September 14, 2026 at 7:00pm. This meeting was held at the Hamilton Wenham Library, 14 Union Street and on HWCAM. This meeting was recorded. The Select Board functions as the Chief Executive body of the Town. Its five members are elected to three-year terms with one or two seats up for election each year. The Board acts as the chief policy making body of the Town and directly supervises the activities of the Town Manager. The Select Board typically meets the first and third Monday evening at 7:00 p.m. Select Board: Lee McCoy (2029); Ben Galuza (2028); Thomas Myers (2028); William Olson (2027); Rosemary Kennedy (2027). Call to order: Vice-Chair T.Myers called the meeting to order and took roll call. Present: L.McCoy, R.Kennedy, B.Galuza (via zoom). Not present: W.Olson. Also present: Joe Domelowicz, Town Manager, and others as noted. The Chair announced Board and Committee openings as displayed on the agenda: • Affordable Housing Trust (AHT)– 1 opening • Conservation Commission (CC) – 1 opening • Community Preservation Committee (CPC)– 2 openings • Hamilton Environmental Impact Committee (HEIC) – 1 opening • Council on Aging (COA) – 1 opening • Historic District Commission (HDC) - 2 openings for 3-year terms, 2 openings for 2-year terms • Human Rights Commission (HRC) – 1 at-large opening • Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) – 1 opening • Public Comment – Will be taken for a maximum of (30) minutes, no speaker will be allowed to speak for more than (3) minutes: o Maryann Cannon of the Friends of the HW Library invited the Board to the Friends of the Library Gala Fundraiser on November 13 at First Church in Wenham, with a silent auction and other activities. • Select Board Committee Liaison Reports: o R.Kennedy attended the Zoning Board meeting. The newest member participated, and the negotiations continued on 957 Bay Rd in Executive Session. The town’s tree project is in the final phases. She is in touch with David Smith from the Board of Health to meet to discuss the e-bike issue. o L.McCoy stated that the Hamilton Dark Sky group continues their work and is drafting a bylaw. He attended the HDC meeting and noted there is new member interested in joining, perhaps as an associate. Wenham has a survey open about Pingree Park which is open to Hamilton residents as well. o B.Galuza noted that he is collecting feedback on the capital planning policy, and it will come to the Board after he has received the external input. CONSENT AGENDA: • Approve banner at Council on Aging for Fall Book Sale • Approve use of Patton Park for Essex County Trail Association annual 5K run Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call to accept the consent agenda. • Approve minutes of the August 17, 2026 Select Board Meeting Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call to approve the minutes as edited. AGENDA: • Department Head Report – Presentation from Chief Edward Guy and Captain Matt Donovan on Hamilton Police Department Traffic Enforcement Program and discussion with Select Board Police Chief Guy spoke on traffic enforcement, noting this is usually the number one issue in communities, including Hamilton. He stressed it is important to understand how the police department operates to keep the town safe. Education is the most important thing with operating motor vehicles, which they prefer to focus on most. Enforcement and education programs are designed to change illegal and dangerous behavior and to promote voluntary compliance with the laws of the Select Board Meeting minutes 9.14.26 Page 1 of 3 . Commonwealth. Police use data to target areas where resources will be most effective, and they aim to foster a safe driving environment. He explained how various strategies are used and how behaviors such as speeding or distracted driving are targeted for enforcement action; the system including verbal warnings, written warnings that are logged, civil citations, criminal complaints, and arrest; the process officers use to evaluate a situation, and the discretion officers are given. He clarified that if it illegal to have quotas for traffic stops. Chief Guy invited the community to express their concerns about traffic problems or other issues to the police. He spoke on staffing challenges and gave statistics on the department, such as 5,361 traffic stops between January and September 2026. During brief questions from the Board, he again encouraged people to reach out to the police with problems or incidents that they are seeing. He identified that issues with Route 1A have to be raised with the State. T.Myers asked about the recent break-ins to vehicles in people’s driveways and Chief responded that there are groups who travel around to places like Hamilton where cars may not be secured. The police department believed it was one group circulating through Beverly, Ipswich, and Hamilton. A person of interest was pursued but was not apprehended, and they determined that it was a group of three people. He urged people to secure their vehicles and have situational awareness. He invited everyone to Public Safety Day on Saturday from 10-2. There was further discussion about the issues at the intersection of Essex and Woodbury, and possible solutions, but that also includes a State road and would require State involvement and authorization. • Approve Early Voting Hours through Town Clerk’s Office for November General Election J.Domelowicz reviewed the memo from Town Clerk Karin Cale on her request for approval of early voting hours. Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call to approve the early voting hours as suggested by Karin Cale. • Appoint Ashley Serotta as member Hamilton Wenham Cultural Council – Discussion & Vote A.Serotta introduced herself as having lived in Hamilton for 10 years and would like to be more involved in the community. The Board thanked her for volunteering. Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call to approve Ashley Serotta as a member of the Cultural Council. • Appoint Jean Pagliuca as a member of the Council on Aging to fill the unexpired term of a vacant seat. J.Pagliuca explained that she currently works for Senior Care and is interested in joining the Council on Aging. Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call to approve Jean Pagliuca as a member of the Council on Aging. • Appoint Elizabeth Ford as an associate member of the Council, on Aging for a term of two (2) years E.Ford introduced herself and noted that she has been volunteering at the COA and would like to be more involved. She noted the great things happening at the COA, and she hopes to use her background in marketing to spread the word. Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call to approve Elizabeth Ford as an associate member of the Council on Aging for a 2-year term. • Second Reading of the revised Cemetery Plot Purchase Policy - Select Board member Rosemary Kennedy R.Kennedy noted that she made two changes since the last reading, clarifying that the person who wants to buy the plot and their significant other are eligible, and to change the criteria for a resident who moves out of town. She read the new language aloud for the Board to consider. R.Kennedy will make the edit requested, and it will be on the next meeting agenda for a vote. • Discussion on next policies to be updated with general timeline – Select Board J.Domelowicz asked for an update of the policies that the Board is planning to work on so he can be prepared to assist with the process. R.Kennedy noted that she is working on e-bikes, and the use of facilities, such as Town Hall. B.Galuza raised the issue of a policy on temporary signage, and he is currently working on the capital planning policy. There was a brief discussion about discussion and deliberation between Board members under State rules, and the need to post group meetings even if there is not a quorum. There was discussion of different permutations of how working groups could be constructed. T.Myers will consult with each Board member to construct a full list of what policies everyone is working on to provide to J.Domelowicz. • Final Discussion & Vote on the FY27 Town Manager & Select Board Goals The Board continued their discussion of the Board goals for FY27. J.Domelowicz noted that the current iteration is in the packet, and is rank prioritized. He will incorporate additional feedback if received. Some goals require additional specificity, such as for economic development. R.Kennedy suggested a joint meeting with the Planning Board to talk about economic development and the goals related to the master plan implementation. The Board committed to everyone submitting their rank ordering prior to the next meeting. There was discussion about assessing town facilities and how that might be done and in Select Board Meeting minutes 9.14.26 Page 2 of 3 . what format. J.Domelowicz stated that the town departments do this already in some fashion for the facilities they have responsibility for, and it feeds into the capital budget process. • Discussion on FY 2028 budget goals guidance for department heads & the GFOA Budget document J.Domelowicz asked for feedback on the proposed budget goals, which will be finalized at the next meeting. There was some discussion of longer-range financial goals, but J.Domelowicz discussed the challenges of trying to look long term in the municipal setting where much is tied to market conditions and a single revenue source. • • • • • New Business (Discussion of items to place on a future agenda) T.Myers asked that DPW Director be invited in soon to do an update on road maintenance and other DPW updates. T.Myers expressed concern about the potential for cybersecurity issues, and asked for the IT collaborative and/or consultant to provide an update on cybersecurity. L.McCoy noted businesses have reached out to him about improved signage and wayfinding downtown, and asked about working with the HDC and/or others. J.Domelowicz will get back to him with further information about the project that is in the planning phases. J.Domelowicz noted he has drafted the calendar of meeting dates leading up to Town Meeting. Adjournment: Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call adjourn the meeting at approximately 9:20PM. Also present: Joe Domelowicz, Town Manager, and others as noted. The plan is to coach and educate people about low phosphorous upgrades as their septic systems fail or come up for replacement, and to build an action plan. Chair Olson asked D.Lash to draft the letter of support for the Board’s review at the next meeting. • Select Board Committee Liaison Reports: B. Galuza noted that he is working on the Capital Planning Policy and has received feedback from the Capital Planning Committee. He also provided an update from the Finance Committee, which recently received a presentation from Hamilton-Wenham Regional School District Superintendent Eric Tracy regarding the School District’s strategic plan. He noted that the Town should expect a request from the School District for an article on the Annual Town Meeting warrant to assist with funding a facilities audit. He also noted other potential warrant articles i.e. a fund transfer for recreational fields, as well as for potential financial impacts associated with updating the school agreement and developing water sources and interconnections with Wenham. L.McCoy met with the Human Rights Committee that is working on a land acknowledgement and an Indigenous People’s Day event. Public Safety Day and the Children’s Business Fair were both great events recently held in town. Chair Olson noted that the Town Hall renovations are nearly complete and that staff will be moving back into Town Hall shortly. A couple of additional inspections are still pending. o o o CONSENT AGENDA: • Essex County Trail Association (ECTA) Trails Event - Request to place signs for the trail run J. text: COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS WILLIAM FRANCIS GALVIN SECRETARY OF THE COMMONWEALTH WARRANT FOR 2026 STATE ELECTION SS. To the Constables of the City/Town of HAMPDEN GREETINGS: In the name of the Commonwealth, you are hereby required to notify and warn the inhabitants of said city or town who are qualified to vote in Elections to vote at: _ 0/001 __ TOWN HALL 85 WILBRAHAM ROAD On TUESDAY, THE THIRD DAY OF NOVEMBER, 2026, from 7:00 A.M. to 8:00 P.M. for the following purpose: To cast their votes in the State Election for the candidates for the following offices and questions: SENATOR IN CONGRESS For this Commonwealth GOVERNOR and LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR For this Commonwealth ATTORNEY GENERAL For this Commonwealth SECRETARY OF STATE For this Commonwealth TREASURER For this Commonwealth AUDITOR For this Commonwealth REPRESENTATIVE IN CONGRESS FIRST DISTRICT COUNCILLOR EIGHTH DISTRICT SENATOR IN GENERAL COURT HAMPDEN, HAMPSHIRE & WORCESTER DISTRICT REPRESENTATIVE IN GENERAL COURT SECOND HAMPDEN DISTRICT DISTRICT ATTORNEY HAMPDEN DISTRICT REGISTER OF PROBATE HAMPDEN COUNTY QUESTION 1: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. This proposed law would exempt documents related to the development of public policy and communications between legislators and their constituents, if those communications are reasonably related to a constituent’s request for assistance in obtaining government-provided benefits or services or interacting with a government agency. A YES VOTE would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. A NO VOTE would make no change to the Massachusetts Public Records Law. QUESTION 2: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would specify that employees of the Committee for Public Counsel Services (“CPCS”) are permitted to engage in collective bargaining with their employer. It would also require CPCS, after executing a collective bargaining agreement, to request the appropriation necessary to fund such agreement from the Governor. A YES VOTE would specify that Committee for Public Counsel Services employees may form a union to collectively bargain with their employer. A NO VOTE would make no change to the law governing labor relations for Committee for Public Counsel Service employees. QUESTION 3: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would eliminate political party primaries for state elections and instead establish a system where there would be a single, all-party primary in which all candidates, regardless of their party affiliation, would be listed on one ballot, and voters could vote for any candidate on the ballot. The two candidates receiving the most votes in the primary would advance to the general election ballot. This proposed law would require candidates for governor and lieutenant governor to run and be listed jointly on the ballot in the primary. This proposed law would provide political party status to any group whose candidates for any statewide office received at least 3% of the ballots cast in the state primary. A YES VOTE would eliminate separate party primaries for state elections and require a single primary in which all candidates appear on one ballot, voters could vote for any candidate, and the top two candidates would advance to the general election. A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing primary elections. QUESTION 4: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would permit eligible individuals to register to vote or update their voter registration address on Election Day. An individual who is eligible to vote could register to vote on Election Day by going to the polling place in the precinct where they live during voting hours and presenting proof of residency and signing a written oath. Proof of residency could be a valid photo identification, or documentation showing the individual’s name and the address where the individual resides, such as a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, residential lease, wireless telephone statement, paycheck, current student fee statement or other document from a post-secondary school, or another government document or correspondence. The written oath would require the individual to certify that they are a citizen of the United States, are at least 18 years old, are not legally prohibited from voting, and have not and will not vote in the same election 2 at another location. The oath would require the individual to acknowledge that providing false information is a felony punishable by not more than 5 years imprisonment or a fine of not more than $10,000, or both. If an individual did not present proof of residency, they would be allowed to cast a provisional ballot, which would be counted only if the individual returned to provide the required information before the close of polls for a municipal election; within two days after a state primary; or within six days after a state election. Individuals who register to vote on Election Day would be registered to vote in future elections as well as in the election taking place that day. Individuals who are already registered to vote would not be able to change their political party affiliation on Election Day. The proposed law would take effect on January 1, 2028. A YES VOTE would permit eligible citizens to register to vote or to update their voter registration address at their polling place on Election Day. A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing voter registration. QUESTION 5: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would change the limit on how much revenue the state can collect in a given year. The proposal would limit state revenue in a given year to the net amount of state revenue from the year before, increased by a rate equal to the average growth of wages and salaries in Massachusetts over the most recent three years. If revenue collected by the state in a given year exceeds the limit, the excess amount would be refunded to taxpayers the following year. The proposed law would include all revenue from the surtax on incomes over $1 million when calculating the revenue limit and when determining whether state revenue exceeds the limit. The provisions of the proposed law would all be effective as of July 1, 2027. The proposed law states that, if any of its parts were declared invalid, the other parts would stay in effect. A YES VOTE would change the limit on state revenue collection, tying it to prior year collections plus average wage and salary growth, and provide for a rebate of revenue exceeding that limit. A NO VOTE would make no change in the law relative to state revenue collection. QUESTION 6: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would establish a Nature for All Fund that, subject to appropriation by the Legislature, would receive 50% of state taxes collected from the sale and use of sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses for the first year of its operation. After July 1, 2028, the Nature for All Fund would begin receiving, subject to appropriation by the Legislature, 100% of state taxes collected on the sale and use of sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses. The sales tax revenue received by the Nature for All Fund would exclude sales tax revenue transferred to the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority State and Local Contribution Fund and the School Modernization and Reconstruction Trust Fund. The proposed law would allow the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to spend the money in the Nature for All Fund for natural resource conservation. 3 The proposed law would allow public and private donations to the Nature for All Fund. The proposed law would prevent the state comptroller from transferring surplus funds in the Nature for All Fund at the end of the fiscal year. It would also allow state agencies, municipalities, public charities involved in natural resource conservation, tribal governments, and other regional public entities to receive money from the Nature for All Fund. Natural resource conservation would include the conservation or restoration of land to protect drinking water, streams, rivers, lakes, coasts, farms, forests, connectivity between open spaces, and lands and natural resources of indigenous cultural significance. Natural resource conservation would also include the creation, improvement, and management of parks, trails, greenspaces or outdoor recreation access. The proposed law would establish a 15-member Nature for All Board that consists of five state officials and ten members of the public appointed by the Governor. The proposed law would require the ten members of the public to include representatives of underserved communities and indigenous peoples and at least one person with expertise or experience in natural resource conservation. The proposed law would allow the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to spend money from the Nature for All Fund to hire staff to manage the fund. The proposed law would also require the Nature for All Board to establish rules about how the money in the Nature for All Fund should be spent, including rules regarding alignment with environmental justice principles, access to and restoration of lands and natural resources of indigenous cultural significance, promotion of affordable housing development, and other matters regarding spending and bond issuance. The proposed law would require the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to submit an annual report to various state committees regarding the funds spent to buy or improve land in cities and towns containing environmental justice populations. The proposed law would take effect on July 1, 2027. A YES VOTE would create a fund that could be utilized for natural resource conservation that would receive some state taxes collected on the sale and use of sporting goods and recreational vehicles, and the use of golf courses. A NO VOTE would not create this natural resource conservation fund or change how sales and use taxes are spent. QUESTION 7: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would allow single-family homes to be built in a residentially zoned area as long as the land on which it is to be constructed is at least 5,000 square feet, has at least 50 feet of land bordering the street, road, or public way that it faces, and has access to public sewer and water services. The proposed law would allow cities and towns to reasonably regulate certain aspects of those single-family homes, including their height, distance from neighboring buildings, open space, parking requirements, and whether they can be rented out on a short-term basis. The proposed law would also allow the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities to issue guidance or regulations to administer the proposed law. A YES VOTE would allow single-family homes to be built on lots of 5,000 square feet or more in residential areas, subject to reasonable local regulation of certain aspects of those homes. A NO VOTE would make no change to the law relative to building single-family homes. QUESTION 8: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY The proposed law would change the type and amount of marijuana that may legally be possessed in Massachusetts by repealing the laws that legalize, regulate, and tax the retail sale of adult recreational use marijuana in Massachusetts. The proposed law would also permit persons 21 years of age and older to possess 1 ounce or less of marijuana including no more than 5 grams in the form of concentrate, and to gift or transfer to another person 21 years of age and older 1 ounce or less of marijuana including no more than 5 grams in the form of concentrate. The proposed law would also impose a civil penalty of $100 and forfeiture of the marijuana for the possession of marijuana between the weight of 1 and 2 ounces. For persons 21 years of age and younger, the proposed law would make the possession of 2 ounces or less of marijuana a civil infraction subject to a $100 fine, forfeiture of the marijuana, completion of a drug awareness program and community service, and notification to their parents or legal guardian of the offense and penalties. The proposed law would allow currently licensed adult recreational marijuana businesses to apply on an expedited basis to become a licensed medical marijuana dispensary and to sell their remaining inventory of adult recreational marijuana to medical marijuana dispensaries. The proposed law would retain the Cannabis Control Commission but modify its authority so it would regulate only the medical marijuana market. The proposed law states that, if any of its parts were declared invalid, the other parts would stay in effect. The proposed law would take effect on January 1, 2028. A YES VOTE would prohibit the legalization, regulation, and taxation of the retail sale of adult recreational use marijuana, and change the penalties for possession of marijuana. A NO VOTE would make no change to the law relative to marijuana. QUESTION 9: REFERENDUM ON AN EXISTING LAW Do you approve of a law summarized below, which was approved by the House of Representatives on July 18, 2024 by a vote of 124 to 33, and approved by the Senate on July 18, 2024 by a vote of 35 to 5? SUMMARY This law makes a number of changes to Massachusetts laws governing firearms. The law adds school administrators and licensed healthcare providers as parties permitted to ask a court to issue an Extreme Risk Protection Order — requiring an individual to surrender or relinquish their firearm licenses, permits, and firearms - if an individual is a present danger to self or others. The law also provides that, when issuing an Harassment Prevention Order, a court may also order the surrender of firearms licenses, permits, and firearms. The law imposes penalties for possessing, creating, and transferring untraceable “ghost gun” firearms and requires all firearms except antiques and relics, including unfinished frames and receivers that can be readily made into a finished product, to have serial numbers. The law includes privately-made guns like 3D-printed guns within the provisions governing untraceable “ghost gun” firearms. The law changes firearms licensing requirements to: (1) allow local licensing authorities to request prior license and permit information from the state, as well as access petitions for involuntary mental health commitments denied by a court in addition to prior involuntary commitments, as a part of their review of applications for licenses to carry firearms, firearm ID cards, and licenses to sell firearms; (2) require an individual to be 21 years of age to own semiautomatic rifles or shotguns; (3) add the possibility of incarceration of up to six months for a second offense of failing to report a firearm loss or theft; and (4) enable 12-15 year olds to apply for a self-defense spray permit with parental permission, and 15 to 18 year olds to apply independently. The law allows local firearm licensing authorities to transfer the responsibility to inspect firearm dealers to the State Police. The law requires local licensing authorities to attend statewide training regarding those inspections. It requires dealers to confiscate expired or suspended licenses and report them to the state and to local licensing authorities. The law changes the definition of “machine gun” to include bump stocks, trigger cranks, Glock switches and auto sears among the devices whose possession and use are subject to penalties. It expands the definition of “silencer” to include the parts used to construct a silencer. The law clarifies how to determine whether a firearm is an assault-style weapon and the circumstances under which a person may continue to possess assault-style weapons and large capacity feeding devices they already own. The law requires the state Firearm Control Advisory Board and the state Secretary of Public Safety and Security to review and update the rosters of prohibited assault-style firearms, approved firearms, and approved firearms sold for target shooting. The law clarifies requirements relating to the carry and transport of firearms in motor vehicles and ATVs. It prohibits the carrying of firearms in government buildings, polling locations, and schools, with certain exceptions. The law expands data compilation and reporting requirements to and from the state, and creates a publicly-accessible dashboard of anonymized aggregate firearm data, along with a commission to study that data. The law requires the State Police to provide training and a test for new applicants for licenses to carry or Firearm ID cards. The law establishes two special legislative commissions — one to examine funding for violence prevention services, and one to study emerging firearms technology. The law criminalizes discharging a firearm and striking a building in use. A YES VOTE would keep in place the law, which increases the regulation of firearms, including ghost guns, machine guns, and assault-style weapons. A NO VOTE would repeal this law. During this time, the Commission will hear a Notice of Intent filed by the applicant/property owner, Zeeshan Sheikh, 109 Maple Street LLC, for the raze and rebuild of a single-family dwelling and associated site appurtenances within the 200-foot Riverfront Area, within the 100-foot Buffer Zone to Bank, and Bordering Vegetated Wetlands and Bordering Land Subject to Flooding (Local Code), located at 109 Maple Street, Assessors Map 38, Lot 37, in Lexington, MA. Plans are available for inspection through Lexington’s online permitting system, OpenGov, No. CNOI-26-27. (Go to https://lexingtonma.portal.opengov.com/search and search by Records). The Conservation Commission Agenda with the virtual meeting link will be posted 48 hours in advance at https://www.lexingtonma.gov/AgendaCenter. If this hearing is not closed, it will continue to a date requested by the applicant without further abutters notification. Ruth Ladd, Chair Conservation Commission
