title: Special Town Meeting Warrant
text: Town of Mansfield SPECIAL TOWN MEETING WARRANT November 12, 2026 MANSFIELD HIGH SCHOOL 250 East Street Mansfield CALL TO ORDER: 7:00 PM Town of Mansfield WARRANT FOR THE SPECIAL TOWN MEETING Thursday, November 12, 2026 BRISTOL, SS: To either of the Constables of the Town of Mansfield in the County of Bristol; GREETINGS: IN THE NAME OF THE COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS, you are hereby directed to notify and warn the inhabitants of said town, qualified to vote in elections and in town affairs, to meet at the Mansfield High School Auditorium, 250 East Street, Mansfield, Mansfield, Massachusetts (Precincts One, Two, Two-A, Three, Four, Five, Six, Six-A and Seven) in said Mansfield on Thursday, November 12, 2026 at Seven O’clock in the afternoon, at the said Mansfield High School Auditorium, or some other convenient date and time, then and there to act on the following articles: Article 1: To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate or transfer from available funds to further amend, increase, decrease, or otherwise adjust the appropriations voted at the May 5, 2026 Annual Town meeting for several Municipal Town departments for Fiscal Year 2027, or take any other action relative thereto. Explanation: At the time the appropriations were voted at the May 5, 2026 Annual Town Meeting, many assumptions were made in order to balance the various budgets. This article (if approved) would allow the Town to now further amend, increase, decrease, or otherwise adjust these appropriations based upon new information not previously known. This article will seek additional funding for Budget 610 Public Library, Budget 152 Public Buildings, and Budget 131 Finance Committee. If approved, the additional $18,442 library funding will satisfy the Municipal Appropriations Requirement (MAR) per Massachusetts General Law Chapter 78 Section 19A to maintain eligibility to receive State Aid to Public Libraries. Without the funding the Town would be required to file a waiver from the state. The FY2026 budget required a waiver to be filed. If approved, the $60,000 funding for Public Facilities Maintenance will allow the Town to restore funding for routine maintenance and inspections for town-owned buildings that was previously cut in the creation of the FY2027 budget. If approved, the Finance Committee’s Reserve fund will be further funded by an additional $250,000. Pursuant to the Town’s Reserve Fund policy, the Town shall endeavor to fund the Finance Reserve at a rate of 1% of the operating budget minus debt, which constitutes about $540,000 for FY2027. Page 1 of 21 Article 2: To see if the Town will vote to amend Chapter 52 of the General Bylaws, Revolving Funds, by adding the following revolving funds to the table contained in § 52-5: Revolving Fund Name Programs and Purposes of Fund Departmental Officer Fiscal Year Receipts to be Authorized to Credited to Fund Expend from Fund District Expenses of District All advertising Superintendent Fiscal Year Advertising programs, fees, of Schools 2027 and activities, events, sponsorship Sponsorship facilities, payments and publications, other receipts websites, and other received District-sponsored pursuant to initiatives in approved School connection with District which advertising advertising and or sponsorship sponsorship revenue is agreements generated, including related equipment, technology, materials, improvements, and program expenses Animal Materials, supplies Adoption fees Animal Control Fiscal Year Shelter and veterinary care Officer 2028 Needs Fund for animals under the care of the Town or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This Article establishes two new revolving funds: one for School District advertising and sponsorship receipts, and one for animal adoption fee receipts. Because the District Advertising and Sponsorship fund will be funded with a new revenue source that was not available at the beginning of the fiscal year, it may go into effect during the current fiscal year. Accordingly, Article 3 also establishes the current-year expenditure limit for the District Advertising and Sponsorship revolving fund. Because the Animal Shelter Needs revolving fund is funded from an existing revenue source, it cannot become effective until next fiscal year and no expenditure limit is established for the current fiscal year. Page 2 of 21 Article 3: To see if the Town will vote to amend the annual spending limits for the Radio Master Box Fee revolving fund, and establish the Fiscal Year 2027 expenditure limit for the District Advertising and Sponsorship revolving fund, as set forth below: Revolving Fund Name Radio Master Box Fee District Advertising and Sponsorship FY2027 Total Annual Limit on Expenditures from Fund $150,000 $50,000 or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article establishes the annual maximum that is allowed to be expended from these revolving funds. The Radio Master Box Fee account is used for specific purchases related to Fire Suppression systems, alarms and equipment and is under the jurisdiction of the Fire Chief. The established annual upper limit adjustment requested for this fund reflects actual anticipated costs over Fiscal Year 2027. The District Advertising and Sponsorship account is a new revolving fund that will be used for certain School program expenses incurred in connection with activities that generate advertising or sponsorship revenue. Article 4: To see if the Town will raise and appropriate or transfer from available funds a sum of money for deposit into the following funds: Employee Other Post-Employment Benefits (OPEB) Liability Trust Fund; Future Payment of Accrued Liabilities for Compensated Absences Reserve Fund; Town’s Special Education Reserve Fund; or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board for Finance Committee Explanation: The Town is required to pay a percentage of retirees’ medical, dental, and life insurance costs. The Town’s net OPEB liability as of FY2026 is estimated at $135.8 million. This article, if approved, will transfer a sum of money into the OPEB Trust Fund to offset some of those future costs. This article, if approved, will deposit a sum of money into this Reserve Fund and allow the Town Manager to pay compensated absence expenses as outlined in MGL Chapter 50, Section 13D. The qualifying expenses under this account include contractual employment obligations. At the May 2, 2017 Annual Town meeting, voters authorized the creation of a Special Education Reserve Fund for payment of certain Special Education-related expenses. This article, if approved, will deposit a sum of money into this Reserve Fund and allow the Mansfield School Committee, with the approval of the Select Board, to pay Special Education – related expenses per MGL Chapter 40, Section 13E. Page 3 of 21 Article 5: To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, or borrow pursuant to any applicable statute a sum of money for the following Capital Improvement projects for the Town of Mansfield; or take any other action relative thereto. Item Highway Vehicle with Related Equipment Public Safety Radio Upgrades (DPW, MEMA, SCHOOLS, POLICE & FIRE) Town Hall Sidewalk Repair Police Line Cruiser Replacement (3) Fire Cruiser Replacement School District Fire Alarm System Updates/Repairs School Districtwide Buildings and Grounds Maintenance Memorial Park/Plymouth Street Tennis Court Replacement Design Project Memorial Park Parking Lot Repair and Pavement Project SPONSOR: Cost $70,500 Anticipated Funding Source Certified Free Cash $700,000 Certified Free Cash $25,000 $248,000 Certified Free Cash Certified Free Cash $76,000 $200,000 Certified Free Cash Certified Free Cash $400,000 Certified Free Cash $172,000 Certified Free Cash $300,000 Parking Enterprise Retained Earnings Select Board for Capital Improvement Program Committee Explanation: This article will contain several motions to fund the Capital Improvement Program Committee’s recommended Town, School, Sewer Enterprise, Water Enterprise, Airport Enterprise, and Parking Enterprise projects. This article (if approved) will fund the Capital Improvement Program Committee’s recommendations. Article 6: To see if the Town will vote to appropriate a sum of money to pay costs of repairing and/or replacing various roads, sidewalks, public parking and bridges within the Town; and for the payment of all costs incidental and related thereto; to determine whether this appropriation shall be raised by borrowing or otherwise; or to take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board as Road Commissioners Explanation: This article (if approved) will authorize the Treasurer to borrow funds to continue the Town’s work in repairing and replacing roads, sidewalks, parking lots, bridges and other transportation infrastructure throughout the Town. Such funding is used as a supplement to state aid for highway construction and maintenance. Page 4 of 21 Article 7: To see if the Town will vote to transfer from available funds a sum not to exceed Seven Hundred Twenty-Five Thousand Dollars ($725,000) from the Water Enterprise Fund – Retained Earnings to meet the expenses of materials for the Gilbert Street Water Main Project previously authorized by Article 6 of the May 5, 2026 Annual Town Meeting to defray costs related to borrowing funds for said project, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This project was procured in September 2026 and the materials portion of the bid came in lower than originally projected. The Water Enterprise fund has retained earnings available and recently certified by the Department of Revenue. This article allows the Town to fund the materials purchase with available funds and thereby reduce the amount of borrowing required for this project, ultimately reducing associated interest and principal costs. Article 8: To see if the Town will vote transfer from available funds a sum not to exceed Fifty Thousand Dollars ($50,000) to pay for the Town’s Tax Title expenses, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: These funds will be used to meet legal and administrative expenses relative to tax collections and foreclosures, specifically for abandoned properties or those that are in arrears on taxes. Article 9: To see if the Town will vote to transfer a sum of money not to exceed Two Hundred Thousand Dollars ($200,000) from the Sewer Enterprise Fund – Retained Earnings to the Sewer Enterprise Fund – Reserve Fund For Transfer Fund, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article will transfer a sum of money from the Sewer Enterprise Fund’s certified retained earnings into the Sewer Enterprise Fund’s Reserve Fund. It can then be used for any lawful purpose. Article 10: To see if the Town will vote to transfer a sum of money not to exceed Four Hundred Thousand Dollars ($400,000) from the Water Enterprise Fund – Retained Earnings to the Water Enterprise Fund – Reserve Fund For Transfer Fund, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article will transfer a sum of money from the Water Enterprise Fund’s certified retained earnings into the Water Enterprise Fund’s Reserve Fund. It can then be used for any lawful purpose. Page 5 of 21 Article 11: To see if the Town will vote to transfer a sum of money not to exceed Fifty Thousand Dollars ($50,000) from the Airport Enterprise Fund – Retained Earnings to the Airport Enterprise Fund – Reserve Fund For Transfer Fund, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article will transfer a sum of money from the Airport Enterprise Fund’s certified retained earnings into the Airport Enterprise Fund’s Reserve Fund. It can then be used for any lawful purpose. Article 12: To see if the Town will vote to transfer a sum of money not to exceed Seventy-Five Thousand Dollars ($75,000) from the Parking Enterprise Fund – Retained Earnings to the Parking Enterprise Fund – Reserve Fund For Transfer Fund, or take any other action realtive thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article will transfer a sum of money from the Parking Enterprise Fund’s certified retained earnings into the Parking Enterprise Fund’s Reserve Fund. It can then be used for any lawful purpose. Article 13: To see if the Town will vote, pursuant to M.G.L. c. 44 § 53 as amended by c. 77, §§ 9 and 197 of the Acts of 2023, to establish an Opioid Settlement Special Revenue Fund, to be spent under the direction of the Town Manager; and further, to transfer a sum of money not to exceed Five Hundred Forty-Five Thousand Dollars ($545,000.00) previously received from opioid settlements from the Opioid Mitigation Stabilization Fund to said fund; or to take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: The Legislature has authorized municipalities to place opioid settlement receipts in a special revenue fund. The funds may then be expended without further appropriation at the direction of the chief executive officer, only for the purpose identified in said settlement agreements. Mansfield had previously received opioid settlement funds, which had been transferred to the Opioid Mitigation Stabilization Fund, and this article will transfer those funds into the new special revenue fund. Any additional opioid settlement funds received by the Town in the future will be transferred directly to the special revenue fund. Amount in fund as of September 30, 2026 is $540,164.14. Actual amount inclusive of accrued interest will be reflected in motion at Town Meeting. Article 14: To see if the Town will vote to establish the Treasurer/Collector’s fee charged for each written demand issued pursuant to Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 60, Section 15(2), at $30, effective January 1, 2027, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Page 6 of 21 Explanation: This article establishes the fee charged for each written demand for payment of a delinquent tax at $30, the maximum amount permitted by Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 60, Section 15(2). The adjustment is to bring the cost of the fee in line with the administrative costs of managing unpaid tax accounts. Article 15: To see if the Town will vote to accept Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 44, Section 54(b), authorizing trust funds held in the custody of the Treasurer/Collector to be managed as a combined investment pool and invested in accordance with Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 203C, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: Acceptance of this section would permit certain trust funds held in the custody of the Treasurer/Collector to be managed as a combined investment pool and invested in accordance with the “Prudent Investor” standards of Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 203C, rather than the investment limitations otherwise applicable under Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 44, Section 53(a). This provision applies only to qualifying trust funds and does not override investment restrictions contained in a bequest, trust instrument, or other expression of donor intent. Acceptance would provide greater investment flexibility and diversification opportunities with respect to such funds. Article 16: To see if the Town will vote to accept an access easement along Oakland Street for purposes of public use of the existing sidewalk, as shown on the plan titled Sidewalk Easement Plan on file with the Town Clerk’s Office, and further to authorize the Select Board to execute any and all instruments as may be necessary to effectuate the purposes of this article. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article asks voters if they will accept an access easement for purposes of public use of the existing sidewalk which currently traverses into private property. Article 17: To see if the Town will vote to accept a drainage easement on the property at 150 Oakland Street, shown on Assessor’s Map 030 as Parcel 039, owned by 150 Oakland Owner LLC, said easement being shown on the plan titled Drainage & Access Easement Plan on file with the Town Clerk’s Office, and further to authorize the Select Board to execute any and all instruments as may be necessary to effectuate the purposes of this article. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article asks voters if they will accept a drainage easement for such purposes to maintain existing drainage infrastructure which outlets into the Town drainage system located in Oakland Street. Page 7 of 21 Article 18: To see if the Town will vote to amend Chapter 89, Animals, of the General Bylaws, by adding the following two new definitions to section 89-1: DOMESTIC CHARITABLE CORPORATION KENNEL — A facility operated, owned or maintained by a domestic charitable corporation registered with the Department of Agricultural Resources or an animal welfare society or other nonprofit organization incorporated for the purpose of providing for and promoting the welfare, protection and humane treatment of animals, including a veterinary hospital or clinic operated by a licensed veterinarian, which operates consistent with such purposes while providing veterinary treatment and care. VETERINARY KENNEL — a veterinary hospital or clinic that boards dogs for reasons in addition to medical treatment or care; provided, however, that ''veterinary kennel'' shall not include a hospital or clinic used solely to house dogs that have undergone veterinary treatment or observation or will do so only for the period of time necessary to accomplish that veterinary care. and by amending subsections of sections 89-3, 89-5, 89-6, 89-8 and 89-13 as follows (additions show in bold and underline and deletions shown in strikethrough): § 89-3. Animal Control Officer. E. Review all dogs that have not been licensed by their owners and report findings to the Animal Welfare Committee/Animal Control OfficerTown Clerk on a monthly basis. § 89-5. Permits. A. No person, partnership, or corporation shall operate a commercial animal establishment, kennel, or animal shelter without first obtaining a permit in compliance with this section. C. A permit shall be issued by the licensing authority upon payment of the applicable fee and when a permit applicant has shown that they are willing and able to comply with the regulations promulgated by the permit granting authority and the Massachusetts Department of Agricultural Resources, and an inspection of facility has been satisfactorily completed by the Animal Control Officer and signed off by the Animal Welfare Committee/Chief of Police. F. If there is a change in ownership of a commercial animal establishment or kennel, within 30 days the new owner must have the current permit transferred to their name upon payment of a transfer fee of $10 after the Animal Control Officer has inspected the premises. A Public Hearing will be held by the MARSHFIELD ZONING BOARD OF APPEALS on Tuesday, November 24th, 2026 at 6:30 P.M. to consider the following: #26-60: Blake Cuneo – The Petitioner is seeking a Variance in accordance with § 305-10.11 of the Marshfield Municipal Code for an existing lot configuration providing approximately 4,500 feet of frontage that is non-continuous with an additional 58.07 feet of frontage, where 125 feet of continuous frontage is required. The property also narrows to approximately 20.1 feet in width at a point between the front lot line and the rear building line, where the applicable minimum lot width is 125 feet. The Petitioners and all interested parties are advised to check the Town website and/or Zoning Board of Appeals homepage for additional information and details. All or any of the members of the public body may choose to participate in a public meeting via remote access. Meetings may be virtual, in their entirety. 2. The public will not be allowed into a Board/Committee meeting, even when there are any members of the public body and/or town staff or official(s) physically present at the meeting location during the meeting. “Public comment” portions of meetings will be temporarily suspended. 3. However, the public will be provided with alternative access through which they can watch or listen to meetings “in real time,” and meeting notices will specify the manner in which members of the public may access audio or video of the meeting as it is occurring. 4. Notices for public hearings will contain additional information about how the public may participate via electronic/technological means. 6. For executive session meetings, public access to the meeting will be limited to the open session portion(s) of the meeting only. Public access to any audio, video, internet or web-based broadcast of the meeting will be discontinued when the public body enters executive session. 7. Where individuals have a right, or are required, to attend a public meeting or hearing, including executive session meetings, they will be provided with information about how to participate in the meeting/hearing remotely. 8. Meeting notices will still be posted at least 48 hours in advance (not counting Saturdays, Sundays, or legal holidays), unless it is an emergency meeting as defined under the Open Meeting Law (in which event, the meeting notice will be posted with as much advanced notice as is possible in the circumstances). ---PUBLIC HEARING GUIDELINES The meeting will be conducted with decorum. This means that the members of the Commission and the public are required to respect each other at all times. We may not always agree with one-another but we can work to resolve differences with patience and understanding. As a member of the public, your questions will be answered in an orderly manner IF you follow these procedures: (1) Raise your hand to be recognized. All those who wish to be heard will be heard. (2) Direct all questions to the Commission through the Chair. (3) Limit your questions and statements to five (5) minutes. After everyone has had a turn to speak, you may be given a second chance to speak, time permitting. (4) Limit your statements/questions to the applicant’s project. (5) Talk ONLY about issues that are under the jurisdiction of the Conservation Commission. These include issues dealing with wetlands, the ocean, streams, quarries, and vernal pools, among many others. The commission DOES NOT have authority over building heights, zoning issues, rights of way, property ownership, or historic structures, to mention but a few. The order of discussion is as follows: (1) The applicant will make his/her presentation. (2) The Conservation Commission will question the applicant. (3) The public will then be given time to ask questions about the project. The commission will then either: (a) conclude that they have sufficient information and close the hearing: No new information will be accepted except under extra ordinary conditions, or (b) the hearing will be continued to a date certain where all will be permitted to participate. The date and time of this continuance will be announced ONLY at the first and subsequent meetings. You have the right to record any session of this meeting if you inform the chairman prior to the session. If you have any questions about procedures, please feel free to contact our agent, John Lopez at 978-546-5005 during regular office hours, which are Monday through Wednesday 9:30 AM – 12:00 PM and Thursday 12:00-3:00 PM. The volunteer members of the Rockport Conservation Commission work for the people of Rockport. Please help us serve you better by keeping us and yourselves informed. Mel Higgins Chair

Vote that the Town Council of the Town of Southbridge in the Exercise of powers conferred on it by Section 8 of Article LXXXIX of the amendments to the state constitution and by its own home rule charter does hereby adopt and enact the following: Amend the Town of Southbridge Zoning Bylaws Bylaw Section 10.1 Definitions by adding the definition of Data Center. Town Council Agenda Page 2 of 4 25. Data Center: A facility or campus consisting of one or more buildings primarily used for housing, operating, and co-locating networked computer systems, servers, data storage systems, and telecommunications equipment. The primary land-use intent of the facility is the remote processing, continuous management, physical storage, and global dissemination of digital data, information, or high-performance artificial intelligence model training and machine learning computation. This definition explicitly applies to hyperscale data centers, enterprise data centers, co-location facilities, edge data centers, server farms, modular or containerized data systems, and cryptocurrency or blockchain mining operations (only where such activity constitutes the principal use of the premises.) This definition excludes standard, localized IT rooms, server closets, or computer infrastructure that is secondary, subordinate, and customarily incidental to an otherwise permitted use on the property (e.g., standard server rooms supporting an individual office building, medical complex, school, or retail store) Vote that the Town Council of the Town of Southbridge in the Exercise of powers conferred on it by Section 8 of Article LXXXIX of the amendments to the state constitution and by its own home rule charter does hereby adopt and enact the following: Amend the Town of Southbridge Zoning Bylaws Section 8 Special Regulations, by adding Section 8.11 Temporary Moratorium for Data Centers. 8.11 TEMPORARY MORATORIUM FOR DATA CENTERS 8.11.1 Moratorium. There shall be a 365-day moratorium on the permitting, construction, expansion, conversion, establishment, or operation of any Data Center in the Town. This moratorium shall begin no earlier than fourteen days following the Town Council’s adoption of this zoning by-law. 8.11.2 No applications. During the moratorium, no application, permit, special permit, site plan, variance, building permit, zoning permit, or other land use approval shall be accepted, processed, or approved for a Data Center. 8.11.3 Pending applications. Any pending application for a Data Center shall be stayed during the moratorium. 8.11.4 Purpose. The Town Council hereby finds that the rapid development, expansion, and high-density operational characteristics of Data Centers and Data Center Campuses present unique, unprecedented, and accelerating demands on municipal infrastructure, public utilities, and the local environment. As such, the purpose of this temporary moratorium is to establish a reasonable, defined, and limited period during which the Town can pause the review and approval of new Data Center applications. This pause is vital to enable the Town Planning Board, Conservation Commission, and local utility authorities to: (a) Conduct independent studies on the cumulative impacts of data center resource consumption on the local aquifer, municipal water networks, and electrical grid capacity; (b) Develop comprehensive performance standards regarding multi-frequency sound emissions, low-frequency hum mitigation, visual screening, and architectural integration; (c) Review and update the Town Master Plan to ensure that future data center sitings are confined to appropriate zoning overlays that protect residential neighborhoods and natural resources; and (d) Formulate specific ratepayer and environmental protections to ensure that any future data center developments do not impose unfair fiscal burdens or resource degradation upon the residents and businesses of the Town. 8.11.5 Extension. The moratorium may be extended twice for up to 180 days each by the Town Council if it determines that additional time is necessary to complete studies, develop performance standards, review and update the Town Master Plan, or adopt appropriate regulations and zoning by-laws to ensure the protection Town Council Agenda Page 3 of 4 of residents, businesses, natural resources and the environment. The moratorium may be extended by the Town Council if presented with evidence-based justification from the Board of Health, Planning Board, Conservation Committee, Water Department, or utility authorities. 8.11.6 Severability. If any section, subsection, paragraph, sentence, clause, phrase, or provision of this Temporary Moratorium By-Law is for any reason held to be unconstitutional, unlawful, invalid, or unenforceable by a court of competent jurisdiction, such decision shall be confined strictly to the specific provision directly involved in the controversy and the remaining portions of this By-Law shall continue in full force and effect. 26. Town of Hamilton Select Board Meeting Minutes of September 14, 2026 ___ Pursuant to the Open Meeting Law, MGL Chapter 30 A, §§ 18-25, written notice posted by the Town Clerk delivered to all Select Board members, a meeting of the Hamilton Select Board was posted for September 14, 2026 at 7:00pm. This meeting was held at the Hamilton Wenham Library, 14 Union Street and on HWCAM. This meeting was recorded. The Select Board functions as the Chief Executive body of the Town. Its five members are elected to three-year terms with one or two seats up for election each year. The Board acts as the chief policy making body of the Town and directly supervises the activities of the Town Manager. The Select Board typically meets the first and third Monday evening at 7:00 p.m. Select Board: Lee McCoy (2029); Ben Galuza (2028); Thomas Myers (2028); William Olson (2027); Rosemary Kennedy (2027). Call to order: Vice-Chair T.Myers called the meeting to order and took roll call. Present: L.McCoy, R.Kennedy, B.Galuza (via zoom). Not present: W.Olson. Also present: Joe Domelowicz, Town Manager, and others as noted. The Chair announced Board and Committee openings as displayed on the agenda: • Affordable Housing Trust (AHT)– 1 opening • Conservation Commission (CC) – 1 opening • Community Preservation Committee (CPC)– 2 openings • Hamilton Environmental Impact Committee (HEIC) – 1 opening • Council on Aging (COA) – 1 opening • Historic District Commission (HDC) - 2 openings for 3-year terms, 2 openings for 2-year terms • Human Rights Commission (HRC) – 1 at-large opening • Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) – 1 opening • Public Comment – Will be taken for a maximum of (30) minutes, no speaker will be allowed to speak for more than (3) minutes: o Maryann Cannon of the Friends of the HW Library invited the Board to the Friends of the Library Gala Fundraiser on November 13 at First Church in Wenham, with a silent auction and other activities. • Select Board Committee Liaison Reports: o R.Kennedy attended the Zoning Board meeting. The newest member participated, and the negotiations continued on 957 Bay Rd in Executive Session. The town’s tree project is in the final phases. She is in touch with David Smith from the Board of Health to meet to discuss the e-bike issue. o L.McCoy stated that the Hamilton Dark Sky group continues their work and is drafting a bylaw. He attended the HDC meeting and noted there is new member interested in joining, perhaps as an associate. Wenham has a survey open about Pingree Park which is open to Hamilton residents as well. o B.Galuza noted that he is collecting feedback on the capital planning policy, and it will come to the Board after he has received the external input. CONSENT AGENDA: • Approve banner at Council on Aging for Fall Book Sale • Approve use of Patton Park for Essex County Trail Association annual 5K run Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call to accept the consent agenda. • Approve minutes of the August 17, 2026 Select Board Meeting Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call to approve the minutes as edited. AGENDA: • Department Head Report – Presentation from Chief Edward Guy and Captain Matt Donovan on Hamilton Police Department Traffic Enforcement Program and discussion with Select Board Police Chief Guy spoke on traffic enforcement, noting this is usually the number one issue in communities, including Hamilton. He stressed it is important to understand how the police department operates to keep the town safe. Education is the most important thing with operating motor vehicles, which they prefer to focus on most. Enforcement and education programs are designed to change illegal and dangerous behavior and to promote voluntary compliance with the laws of the Select Board Meeting minutes 9.14.26 Page 1 of 3 . Commonwealth. Police use data to target areas where resources will be most effective, and they aim to foster a safe driving environment. He explained how various strategies are used and how behaviors such as speeding or distracted driving are targeted for enforcement action; the system including verbal warnings, written warnings that are logged, civil citations, criminal complaints, and arrest; the process officers use to evaluate a situation, and the discretion officers are given. He clarified that if it illegal to have quotas for traffic stops. Chief Guy invited the community to express their concerns about traffic problems or other issues to the police. He spoke on staffing challenges and gave statistics on the department, such as 5,361 traffic stops between January and September 2026. During brief questions from the Board, he again encouraged people to reach out to the police with problems or incidents that they are seeing. He identified that issues with Route 1A have to be raised with the State. T.Myers asked about the recent break-ins to vehicles in people’s driveways and Chief responded that there are groups who travel around to places like Hamilton where cars may not be secured. The police department believed it was one group circulating through Beverly, Ipswich, and Hamilton. A person of interest was pursued but was not apprehended, and they determined that it was a group of three people. He urged people to secure their vehicles and have situational awareness. He invited everyone to Public Safety Day on Saturday from 10-2. There was further discussion about the issues at the intersection of Essex and Woodbury, and possible solutions, but that also includes a State road and would require State involvement and authorization. • Approve Early Voting Hours through Town Clerk’s Office for November General Election J.Domelowicz reviewed the memo from Town Clerk Karin Cale on her request for approval of early voting hours. Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call to approve the early voting hours as suggested by Karin Cale. • Appoint Ashley Serotta as member Hamilton Wenham Cultural Council – Discussion & Vote A.Serotta introduced herself as having lived in Hamilton for 10 years and would like to be more involved in the community. The Board thanked her for volunteering. Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call to approve Ashley Serotta as a member of the Cultural Council. • Appoint Jean Pagliuca as a member of the Council on Aging to fill the unexpired term of a vacant seat. J.Pagliuca explained that she currently works for Senior Care and is interested in joining the Council on Aging. Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call to approve Jean Pagliuca as a member of the Council on Aging. • Appoint Elizabeth Ford as an associate member of the Council, on Aging for a term of two (2) years E.Ford introduced herself and noted that she has been volunteering at the COA and would like to be more involved. She noted the great things happening at the COA, and she hopes to use her background in marketing to spread the word. Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call to approve Elizabeth Ford as an associate member of the Council on Aging for a 2-year term. • Second Reading of the revised Cemetery Plot Purchase Policy - Select Board member Rosemary Kennedy R.Kennedy noted that she made two changes since the last reading, clarifying that the person who wants to buy the plot and their significant other are eligible, and to change the criteria for a resident who moves out of town. She read the new language aloud for the Board to consider. R.Kennedy will make the edit requested, and it will be on the next meeting agenda for a vote. • Discussion on next policies to be updated with general timeline – Select Board J.Domelowicz asked for an update of the policies that the Board is planning to work on so he can be prepared to assist with the process. R.Kennedy noted that she is working on e-bikes, and the use of facilities, such as Town Hall. B.Galuza raised the issue of a policy on temporary signage, and he is currently working on the capital planning policy. There was a brief discussion about discussion and deliberation between Board members under State rules, and the need to post group meetings even if there is not a quorum. There was discussion of different permutations of how working groups could be constructed. T.Myers will consult with each Board member to construct a full list of what policies everyone is working on to provide to J.Domelowicz. • Final Discussion & Vote on the FY27 Town Manager & Select Board Goals The Board continued their discussion of the Board goals for FY27. J.Domelowicz noted that the current iteration is in the packet, and is rank prioritized. He will incorporate additional feedback if received. Some goals require additional specificity, such as for economic development. R.Kennedy suggested a joint meeting with the Planning Board to talk about economic development and the goals related to the master plan implementation. The Board committed to everyone submitting their rank ordering prior to the next meeting. There was discussion about assessing town facilities and how that might be done and in Select Board Meeting minutes 9.14.26 Page 2 of 3 . what format. J.Domelowicz stated that the town departments do this already in some fashion for the facilities they have responsibility for, and it feeds into the capital budget process. • Discussion on FY 2028 budget goals guidance for department heads & the GFOA Budget document J.Domelowicz asked for feedback on the proposed budget goals, which will be finalized at the next meeting. There was some discussion of longer-range financial goals, but J.Domelowicz discussed the challenges of trying to look long term in the municipal setting where much is tied to market conditions and a single revenue source. • • • • • New Business (Discussion of items to place on a future agenda) T.Myers asked that DPW Director be invited in soon to do an update on road maintenance and other DPW updates. T.Myers expressed concern about the potential for cybersecurity issues, and asked for the IT collaborative and/or consultant to provide an update on cybersecurity. L.McCoy noted businesses have reached out to him about improved signage and wayfinding downtown, and asked about working with the HDC and/or others. J.Domelowicz will get back to him with further information about the project that is in the planning phases. J.Domelowicz noted he has drafted the calendar of meeting dates leading up to Town Meeting. Adjournment: Vote : The Select Board voted unanimously by roll call adjourn the meeting at approximately 9:20PM.
